label: Ques:expansive
title: Question
body_md:
\label{Ques:expansive}
	Does every Fr\'echet space (or locally convex space) support an expansive operator? What about the Fr\'echet space $\omega$?
head: environment

label: Pro:F_n+E_n
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We let $E_0=M$. Fixed any $n \geq 0$, the assumptions imply that $E_{n+1}$ is a closed subspace of finite codimension in $E_n$, so that for each $n \geq 0$ there exists a finite dimensional subspace $F_{n+1}$ fulfilling that $E_n = F_{n+1} \oplus E_{n+1}$.
	
	We \textit{remark} that the subspaces $(F_n)_{n \geq 1}$ can be chosen so that its sequence of valuations $(\operatorname{val}(F_n))_{n \geq 1}$ tends to infinity and thus such that every series $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} f_n$ converges whenever $f_n \in F_n$ for each $n \geq 1$. Indeed, if we consider $k \geq 1$ and $n_k \geq 1$ and we assume that $\operatorname{val}(F_n) \geq k$ for every $n \geq n_k$, then we can show that there exist $n_{k+1} > n_k$ and a choice of $(F_n)_{n \geq n_{k+1}}$ such that $\operatorname{val}(F_n) \geq k+1$ for every $n \geq n_{k+1}$. There are in fact two possible cases:
	\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.]
		\item There exists some $n_{k+1} > n_k$ such that $\operatorname{val}(F_{n}) \geq k+1$ for every $n \geq n_{k+1}$. In this case we have nothing to do.
		
		\item We have that $\operatorname{val}(F_n) = k$ for infinitely many integers $n > n_k$. In this case we enumerate these indices by $(l_j)_{j \geq 1}$ and, recursively, we proceed as follows:
		\begin{enumerate}[label=$\bullet$]
			\item Consider a basis of $F_{l_1}$ containing only one vector $f_{l_1}$ of valuation equal to $k$.
			
			\item Using that $\operatorname{val}(F_{l_2})=k$ and that $F_{l_2} \subset E_{l_1}$, we can find a vector $e_{l_1} \in E_{l_1}$ with valuation equal to $k$.
			
			\item Let $F_{j_1}'$ be the finite dimensional subspace spanned by the basis of $F_{j_1}$ but replacing the vector $f_{l_1}$ by a linear combination of $f_{l_1}$ and $e_{l_1}$ such that its valuation is strictly bigger than $k$. Thus, $\operatorname{val}(F_{l_1}')>k$ and $E_{l_1-1} = F_{l_1}' \oplus E_{l_1}$.
		\end{enumerate}
		Repeating this argument for each $F_{l_j}$ with $j \geq 2$ we obtain a new sequence $(F_{l_j}')_{j \geq 1}$ of finite dimensional subspaces with $\operatorname{val}(F_{l_j}') > k$ and $E_{l_{j-1}} = F_{l_j}' \oplus E_{l_j}$ for all $j \geq 1$. Renaming these spaces by $(F_{l_j})_{j \geq 1}$ and letting $n_{k+1} := n_k+1$ we finally get that $\operatorname{val}(F_n) \geq k+1$ for all $n \geq n_{k+1}$ and that we still have the equality $E_n = F_{n+1} \oplus E_{n+1}$ for all $n \geq 0$, completing the \textit{remark}.\\
	\end{enumerate}
	
	Finally, pick any $x \in M$ and let us show that there exist a unique sequence $(f_n)_{n \geq 1}$, with $f_n \in F_n$ for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and a unique vector $e \in \bigcap_{n \geq 1} E_n$ such that $x = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} f_n + e$. Indeed, by using the fact that $M = F_1 \oplus E_1$ we get unique vectors $f_1 \in F_1$ and $e_1 \in E_1$ such that $x = f_1 + e_1$. Then, since $E_n=F_{n+1}\oplus E_{n+1}$ for every $n \geq 1$, we know that for each $e_n \in E_n$ there exist a unique $f_{n+1} \in F_{n+1}$ and a unique $e_{n+1} \in E_{n+1}$ such that $e_n = f_{n+1} + e_{n+1}$. We thus obtain sequences $(f_n)_{n \geq 1}$ and $(e_n)_{n \geq 1}$, with $f_n \in F_n$ and $e_n \in E_n$ for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, such that
	\[
	x = \sum_{k=1}^n f_k + e_n \quad \text{ for every } n \geq 1.
	\]
	Since the series $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}f_k$ converges, we conclude that the sequence $(e_n)_{n \geq 1}$ is also convergent to some vector $e \in \omega$ and that
	\[
	x = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} f_k + e.
	\]
	Finally, since $(e_n)_{n \geq 1}$ is a convergent sequence and $(E_n)_{n \geq 1}$ is a non-increasing sequence of closed subspaces, we get that $e \in  \bigcap_{n \geq 1} E_n$. Let us remark that we have unicity of both $(f_n)_{n \geq 1}$ and $e$ since, for each $n \geq 1$, the expression
	\[
	x = \sum_{k=1}^{n}f_k + \left( \sum_{k=n+1}^{\infty} f_k + e \right)
	\]
	has to be the unique decomposition of $x$ in the direct sum $\left( \oplus_{k=1}^n F_k \right) \oplus E_n$.
head: environment

label: The:intersect-n>=1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{The:intersect-n>=1}
	For every operator $T$ on $\omega$ and every closed subspace of finite codimension $E \subset \omega$ we have that
	\[
	\bigcap_{n \geq 1} T^{-n}(E) \neq \{0_{\omega}\}.
	\]
head: environment

label: Rem:injectivity
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{Rem:injectivity}
	Before proving Theorem~\ref{The:intersect-n>=1} let us remark that, since 
	\[
	\bigcap_{n \geq 1}T^{-n}(E) = T^{-1}\left(\bigcap_{n \geq 0}T^{-n}(E)\right),
	\]
	it is straightforward to verify that
	\[
	\bigcap_{n \geq 1}T^{-n}(E) \neq \{0_{\omega}\} \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \text{$T$ is not injective \ or \ } \bigcap_{n \geq 0}T^{-n}(E) \neq \{0_{\omega}\}.
	\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $T$ be an operator on $\omega$ and let $E$ be a closed subspace of finite codimension in $\omega$. If $T$ is not injective then we directly get that
	\[
	\{0_{\omega}\} \neq \ker(T) \subset \bigcap_{n \geq 1}T^{-n}(E).
	\]
	Thus, assume that $T$ is injective and notice that, by Remark~\ref{Rem:injectivity}, to complete the proof we must show that $\bigcap_{n \geq 0} T^{-n}(E) \neq \{0_{\omega}\}$. To this end we let $E_0 := \omega$ and
	\[
	E_n := E \cap T^{-1}(E) \cap \cdots \cap T^{-(n-1)}(E) \quad \text{ for each } n \geq 1,
	\]
	so that $(E_n)_{n \geq 1}$ is indeed a non-increasing sequence of closed subspaces of finite codimension in $\omega$. Using Proposition~\ref{Pro:F_n+E_n} we can find a sequence of finite-dimensional subspaces $(F_n)_{n \geq 1}$ such that:
	\begin{enumerate}[label=$\bullet$]
		\item $\omega=F_1\oplus E_1$ and $E_n=F_{n+1}\oplus E_{n+1}$ for every $n \geq 1$;
		
		\item the sequence $(\operatorname{val}(F_n))_{n \geq 1}$ tends to infinity and hence every series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} f_n$ is convergent whenever $(f_n)_{n \geq 1}$ is a sequence with $f_n \in F_n$ for each $n \geq 1$;
		
		\item for every $x \in \omega$ there exist a unique sequence $(f_n)_{n \geq 1}$, with $f_n\in F_n$ for each $n \geq 1$, and a unique vector $e \in \bigcap_{n \geq 1} E_n$ such that $x = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} f_n + e$.\\
	\end{enumerate}
	
	We start noticing that, if there exists $n \geq 0$ such that $E_n=E_{n+1}$, then $E_k = E_n$ for all $k \geq n$. Indeed, if $E_n = E_{n+1}$ and if we consider $k \geq n$ and $x \in E_k$ then we have that $T^{k-n}x \in E_n = E_{n+1}$ and thus we have that $T^nT^{k-n}x = T^kx \in E$. It follows that $x \in E_{k+1}$ and thus that $E_k = E_{k+1}$ for all $k \geq n$. Therefore, if there exists $n \geq 0$ such that $E_n = E_{n+1}$ we would have that
	\[
	\bigcap_{k \geq 0} T^{-k}(E) = E_n \neq \{0_{\omega}\}.
	\]
	Hence, assume that $E_{n+1}$ is a strict subspace of $E_n$ for all $n \geq 0$, which implies that $F_{n+1} \neq \{0_{\omega}\}$ for all $n \geq 0$. Let us check that there exists $N \geq 1$ such that
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:dimF_N}
		\dim(F_n) = \dim(F_N) \quad \text{ for all } n \geq N.
	\end{equation}
	To show this fact notice that given any $n \geq 0$, since $E_{n+1} = F_{n+2}\oplus E_{n+2}$, we have that each $x \in F_{n+2} \setminus \{0_{\omega}\}$ belongs to $E_{n+1}$ but does not belong to $E_{n+2}$, implying that $Tx \in E_n \setminus E_{n+1}$ and hence that $T(F_{n+2}) \subset E_n$ while $T(F_{n+2}) \cap E_{n+1} = \{0_{\omega}\}$. Since $E_n = F_{n+1} \oplus E_{n+1}$, it follows that $\dim(T(F_{n+2})) \leq \dim(F_{n+1})$. Moreover, since we are assuming that $T$ is injective, we deduce that
	\[
	\dim(F_{n+2}) = \dim(T(F_{n+2})) \leq \dim(F_{n+1}).
	\]
	This argument shows that $(\dim(F_n))_{n \geq 1}$ is indeed a decreasing sequence of positive integers, so that there exists some $N \geq 1$ fulfilling \eqref{eq:dimF_N}.
	
	Now we claim that, given any $n \geq N$ and any $x \in E_n$, there exists $(f_k)_{k \geq n+2}$, with $f_k \in F_k$ for each $k \geq n+2$, and a vector $e \in \bigcap_{k \geq 0} T^{-k}(E)$ such that
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:x=T(sum)+e}
		x = T\left( \sum_{k=n+2}^{\infty} f_k \right) + e.
	\end{equation}
	Actually, since $x \in E_n$ we have that $x = f_{n+1} + e_{n+1}$ for some $f_{n+1} \in F_{n+1}$ and some $e_{n+1} \in E_{n+1}$. Then, using that $T(F_{n+2}) \subset E_n =  F_{n+1} \oplus E_{n+1}$, that $T(F_{n+2}) \cap E_{n+1} = \{0_{\omega}\}$ and that $\dim(T(F_{n+2})) = \dim(F_{n+2}) = \dim(F_{n+1})$, there exists some $f_{n+2} \in F_{n+2}$ such that $Tf_{n+2}-f_{n+1} \in E_{n+1}$. If this was not the case, then the finite-dimensional space $F_{n+1}' := T(F_{n+2}) \oplus \operatorname{span}(f_{n+1})$ would fulfill that $\dim(F_{n+1}') = \dim(T(F_{n+2}))+1 > \dim(F_{n+1})$ while $F_{n+1}' \cap E_{n+1} = \{0_{\omega}\}$, which contradicts that $\dim(F_{n+1})$ is the codimension of $E_{n+1}$ as a subspace of $E_n$. It follows that $x=Tf_{n+2}+e'_{n+1}$ for some $e'_{n+1}\in E_{n+1}$. Repeating the argument for the vector $e_{n+1}' \in E_{n+1}$ and continuing recursively we get a sequence $(f_k)_{k \geq n+2}$, with $f_k \in F_k$ for each $k \geq n+2$, and a sequence $(e'_k)_{k \geq n+1}$, with $e'_k \in E_k$ for each $k \geq n+1$, such that for every $K \geq n+2$ we have the equality
	\[
	x = \sum_{k=n+2}^{K} Tf_k + e'_{K-1} = T\left( \sum_{k=n+2}^{K} f_k \right) + e'_{K-1} .
	\]
	Since $\sum_{k=n+2}^{\infty}f_{k}$ is convergent by Proposition~\ref{Pro:F_n+E_n}, we finally obtain \eqref{eq:x=T(sum)+e}, where
	\[
	e = \lim_{k \to \infty} e'_k \in \bigcap_{k \geq 0}T^{-k}(E).
	\]
	In particular, \eqref{eq:x=T(sum)+e} implies that $E_n \subset T(E_{n+1}) \oplus \bigcap_{k \geq 0}T^{-k}(E)$ for every $n \geq N$.
	
	Finally, by contradiction, assume that $\bigcap_{k \geq 0}T^{-k}(E)=\{0_{\omega}\}$. Then, by the previous arguments we would have that $E_n \subset T(E_{n+1})$ for every $n \geq N$. Consider the operator $T_N : \oplus_{k=1}^N F_k \longrightarrow \oplus_{k=1}^N F_k$ defined by $T_N := P_N \circ T$, where $P_N$ is the projection of $\omega = (\oplus_{k=1}^N F_k) \oplus E_N$ onto $\oplus_{k=1}^N F_k$. We now have two cases:
	\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.]
		\item If $T_N$ was invertible, then we would have that $T( (\oplus_{k=1}^N F_n) \oplus E_{N+1}) = \omega$. Hence, for every non-zero vector $x \in F_{N+1} \setminus \{0_{\omega}\}$ there would exist another vector $y \in \oplus_{k=1}^N F_n \oplus E_{N+1}$ fulfilling that $Tx = Ty$ while $x \neq y$.
		
		\item If $T_N$ was not invertible, then there would exist a non-zero vector $x \in \oplus_{k=1}^N F_k$ such that $T_Nx=0_{\omega}$. This would mean that $Tx \in E_N$, so that we could find another vector $y \in E_{N+1}$ fulfilling that $Tx = Ty$ while $x \neq y$. 
	\end{enumerate}
	In both cases we get a contradiction with the injectivity of $T$.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md: Let $T$ be an operator on $\omega$. If $T$ is injective and $E$ is a closed subspace of finite codimension in $\omega$, then the operator $T$ admits a non-trivial closed invariant subspace included in $E$.
head: environment

label: The:no.pos-exp.omega
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{The:no.pos-exp.omega}
	There is no (metrically) positively expansive operator on $\omega$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $T$ be an operator on $\omega$. Given $k \in \mathbb{N}$, let
	\[
	E_k := \ker(p_k) = \{ x = ([x]_j)_{j \geq 1} \in \omega : [x]_j = 0 \text{ for } 1 \leq j \leq k \}.
	\]
	It follows from Theorem~\ref{The:intersect-n>=1} applied to the finite-codimensional subspace $E_k$ that there exists some $x \in \omega \setminus \{0_{\omega}\}$ such that $p_{k}(T^nx) = 0$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. By considering an enough small multiple of $x$ we can even assume that $p_{k}(x) < \frac{1}{2^{k}}$. Since $(p_l)_{l \geq 1}$ given by \eqref{eq:omega.seminorms} is an increasing sequence of seminorms, we have for the metric $d$ given by \eqref{eq:metric} and for all $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$ that
	\[
	d(T^nx,0_{\omega}) = \sum_{l=1}^{\infty} \frac{\min\{ 1 , p_l(T^nx) \}}{2^{l}} \leq \frac{1}{2^{k}} \sum_{l=1}^{k} \frac{1}{2^l} + \sum_{l=k+1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{2^l} < \frac{1}{2^{k-1}}.
	\]
	Thus, for each $k \in \mathbb{N}$ there exists some $x \in \omega \setminus \{0_{\omega}\}$ such that $d(T^nx,0_{\omega}) < 2^{-k+1}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$, which shows that $T$ is not positively expansive with respect to $d$.
	
	We also notice that $T$ is not positively expansive with respect to another metric on $\omega$. Actually, if $d'$ is another metric inducing the topology of $\omega$, the equivalence between $d$ and $d'$ implies that for every $c>0$ there exists some $\varepsilon_c>0$ such that we have the open balls inclusion
	\[
	B_{d}(0_{\omega},\varepsilon_c) \subset B_{d'}(0_{\omega},c).
	\]
	Since for every $c>0$ there exists some $x \in \omega \setminus \{0_{\omega}\}$ such that $d(T^nx,0_{\omega})<\varepsilon_c$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$, it follows that $d'(T^nx,0_{\omega})<c$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$. Therefore we deduce that $T$ is not positively expansive with respect to $d'$ and thus that $\omega$ does not admit positively expansive operators (in the metric sense).
head: environment

label: The:intersect-|n|>=L
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{The:intersect-|n|>=L}
	For every invertible operator $T$ on $\omega$ and every closed subspace of finite codimension $E \subset \omega$ there exists some $L \geq 0$ fulfilling that 
	\[
	\bigcap_{|n| \geq L}T^{-n}(E) \neq \{0_{\omega}\}.
	\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $T$ be an invertible operator on $\omega$ and let $E$ be a closed subspace of finite codimension in $\omega$. We let $E_0 := \omega$ and
	\[
	E_n := E \cap T^{-1}(E) \cap \cdots \cap T^{-(n-1)}(E) \quad \text{ for all } n \geq 1,
	\]
	so that $(E_n)_{n \geq 1}$ is indeed a non-increasing sequence of closed subspaces of finite codimension. Using Proposition~\ref{Pro:F_n+E_n} we can find a sequence of finite-dimensional subspaces $(F_n)_{n \geq 1}$ such that:
	\begin{enumerate}[label=$\bullet$]
		\item $\omega=F_1\oplus E_1$ and $E_n=F_{n+1}\oplus E_{n+1}$ for every $n \geq 1$;
		
		\item the sequence $(\operatorname{val}(F_n))_{n \geq 1}$ tends to infinity and hence every series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} f_n$ is convergent whenever $(f_n)_{n \geq 1}$ is a sequence with $f_n \in F_n$ for each $n \geq 1$;
		
		\item for every $x \in \omega$ there exist a unique sequence $(f_n)_{n \geq 1}$, with $f_n\in F_n$ for each $n \geq 1$, and a unique vector $e \in \bigcap_{n \geq 1} E_n$ such that $x = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} f_n + e$.\\
	\end{enumerate}
	
	Now, consider the subspace
	\[
	M := \bigcap_{n \geq 1} E_n = \bigcap_{n \geq 0}T^{-n}(E).
	\]
	We first remark that, if $M$ is a subspace of finite codimension in $\omega$, then by applying Theorem~\ref{The:intersect-n>=1} and Remark~\ref{Rem:injectivity} to the inverse (and hence injective) operator $T^{-1}$ and to the subspace $M$ we would have that
	\[
	\bigcap_{n\in \mathbb{Z}}T^{-n}(E) =\bigcap_{n \geq 0}T^n(M) \neq \{0_{\omega}\}.
	\]
	Therefore we would get the desired result for $L=0$.\\
	
	Thus, let us assume that $M$ is not of finite codimension in $\omega$. In particular, as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{The:intersect-n>=1}, this means that $E_{n+1}$ is a strict subspace of $E_n$ and hence that $F_{n+1}$ is not reduced to $\{0_{\omega}\}$ for all $n \geq 0$. Moreover, since $T$ is invertible and hence injective, again with the same arguments as in Theorem~\ref{The:intersect-n>=1} we can deduce \eqref{eq:dimF_N} and \eqref{eq:x=T(sum)+e}, that is: there exists some $N \geq 1$ such that
	\[
	\dim(F_n) = \dim(F_N) \quad \text{ for all } n \geq N,
	\]
	and given any $n \geq N$ and any $x \in E_n$ there exist a sequence $(f_k)_{k \geq n+2}$, with $f_k \in F_k$ for each $k \geq n+2$, and a vector $m \in M$ such that
	\[
	x = T\left( \sum_{k=n+2}^{\infty}f_k\right ) + m.
	\]
	In particular, from \eqref{eq:x=T(sum)+e} we have that for every $n \geq N$ and every $x\in E_n$ there exist vectors $y \in E_{n+1} \subset E_N$ and $m \in M$ such that
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:Ty+m}
		x = Ty + m.
	\end{equation}
	In addition, using the previous fact multiple times together with the inclusion $T(M) \subset M$ we get that, for every $n \geq N$, every $x\in E_n$ and every $k \geq 1$ there exist vectors $y \in E_{n+k} \subset E_N$ and $m \in M$ such that
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:T^ky+m}
		x=T^ky+m.
	\end{equation}
	These facts \eqref{eq:Ty+m} and \eqref{eq:T^ky+m} will be important to conclude the proof.\\
	
	For each $n \geq 1$ we now let $M_n := M \cap T(M) \cap \cdots \cap T^{n}(M)$, which fulfills that $M_n = T^n(M)$ because $T(M) \subset M$. In particular, we notice that $T(M_n)=M_{n+1}$ and that $M_n$ is of finite codimension in $M$ for every $n \geq 1$ since
	\[
	M_n = T^n(M) = T^n \left(\bigcap_{k \geq 0} T^{-k}(E) \right) = T^n(E_n) \cap M = (T^{-n})^{-1}(E_n) \cap M,
	\]
	and every preimage of a finite codimensional subspace by an operator is again a finite codimensional subspace. We can therefore use Proposition~\ref{Pro:F_n+E_n} for $M$ with the non-increasing sequence of subspaces $(M_n)_{n \geq 1}$ in order to get a family $(G_{n})_{n \geq 1}$ of finite-dimensional subspaces such that:
	\begin{enumerate}[label=$\bullet$]
		\item $M = G_1 \oplus M_1$ and $M_n = G_{n+1} \oplus M_{n+1}$ for every $n \geq 1$;
		
		\item the sequence $(\operatorname{val}(G_n))_{n \geq 1}$ tends to infinity and hence every series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} g_n$ is convergent whenever $(g_n)_{n \geq 1}$ is a sequence with $g_n \in G_n$ for each $n \geq 1$;
		
		\item for every $x \in M$ there exist a unique sequence $(g_n)_{n \geq 1}$, with $g_n \in G_n$ for each $n \geq 1$, and a unique vector $z \in \bigcap_{n \geq 1} M_n$ such that $x = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} g_n + z$.\\
	\end{enumerate}
	
	As in the case in which $M$ was finite codimensional in $\omega$, if we had that
	\[
	\bigcap_{n \geq 0} T^n(M) \neq \{0_{\omega}\}
	\]
	then we would conclude that
	\[
	\bigcap_{n\in \mathbb{Z}} T^{-n}(E) = \bigcap_{n \geq 0} T^n(M) \neq \{0_{\omega}\},
	\]
	getting the desired result for $L=0$. Therefore, assume that $\bigcap_{n \geq 0} T^n(M) = \{0_{\omega}\}$ or, equivalently, that $\bigcap_{n \geq 1} M_n = \{0_{\omega}\}$. A consequence of this assumption is that:
	\begin{enumerate}[label=$\bullet$]
		\item the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} m_n$ is convergent for every sequence $(m_n)_{n \geq 1}$ with $m_n\in M_n$ for each $n \geq 1$.
	\end{enumerate}
	Indeed, since $\bigcap_{n \geq 1} M_n = \{0_{\omega}\}$ we have that each element $m_n \in M_n$ can be written by a series $\sum_{k=n+1}^{\infty} g_k$ with $g_k \in G_k$ for each $k \geq n+1$, and since the sequence of valuations $(\operatorname{val}(G_k))_{k \geq 1}$ tends to infinity we deduce that the sequence of valuations $(\operatorname{val}(M_k))_{k \geq 1}$ also tends to infinity, implying the stated consequence.\\
	
	We now claim that there exist some vector $x \in E_N \setminus M$ and some positive integer $L \geq 1$ fulfilling that $T^L x\in M$. Actually, consider $L \geq 1$ such that
	\[
	\dim(\oplus_{k=1}^N F_k) < \dim(\oplus_{k=N+1}^{N+L} F_k),
	\]
	and let $T_{N,L} : \oplus_{k=N+1}^{N+L} F_k \longrightarrow \oplus_{k=1}^N F_k$ be the operator $T_{N,L} := P_N \circ T^L$, where $P_N$ is the projection of $\omega = (\oplus_{k=1}^N F_k) \oplus E_N$ onto $\oplus_{k=1}^N F_k$. The inequality between the dimensions shows that there exists some vector $z \neq 0_{\omega}$ in the kernel of the finite-dimensional operator $T_{N,L}$, so that
	\[
	z \in \oplus_{k=N+1}^{N+L} F_k \subset E_N \setminus E_{N+L} \quad \text{ and } \quad T^Lz \in E_N.
	\]
	Using~\eqref{eq:T^ky+m} we deduce that there exist vectors $y \in E_{N+L} \subset E_N$ and $m \in M$ with
	\[
	T^Lz=T^Ly+m \quad \text{ and hence } \quad T^{L}(z-y) \in M.
	\]
	Thus, the vector $x = z-y$ belongs to $E_N\setminus M$ while $T^Lx \in M$.\\
	
	To conclude the proof we finally claim that for such vector $x \in E_N \setminus M$ with $T^Lx \in M$, there exists a sequence $(m_n)_{n \geq 0} \subset M$ such that
	\[
	0_{\omega} \neq x-\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}T^{n}m_n \in \bigcap_{|n| \geq L}T^{-n}(E).
	\]
	This sequence $(m_n)_{n \geq 0}$ is obtained recursively. First, using~\eqref{eq:Ty+m} there exist vectors $y_0 \in E_N$ and $m_0 \in M$ such that $x = Ty_0 + m_0$. We then let $x_0 := x-m_0$, so that
	\[
	x_0 \in E_N \subset E \quad \text{ and } \quad T^{-1} x_0 = y_0 \in E_N \subset E.
	\]
	Assume that for some $k \geq 0$ we have already fixed $m_0,\dots,m_k \in M$ such that
	\[
	x_k = x-\sum_{n=0}^k T^{n}m_n
	\]
	satisfies $T^{-l}x_k \in E_N \subset E$ for every $0 \leq l \leq k+1$. Thus, since $T^{-(k+1)}x_k\in E_N$, it follows from~\eqref{eq:Ty+m} that there exist vectors $y_{k+1} \in E_N$ and $m_{k+1} \in M$ such that $T^{-(k+1)}x_k=T y_{k+1}+m_{k+1}$. Letting $x_{k+1} := x_{k}-T^{k+1}m_{k+1} = x-\sum_{n=0}^{k+1}T^{n}m_n$ we have that
	\[
	T^{-l}x_{k+1}=T^{-l}x_k -T^{k+1-l}m_{k+1}\in E_N \subset E \quad \text{  for every } 0 \leq l \leq k+1,
	\]
	but also that
	\[
	T^{-(k+2)} x_{k+1} = T^{-1}(T^{-(k+1)}x_k-m_{k+1}) = y_{k+1} \in E_N \subset E.
	\]
	Recursively we obtain $(x_k)_{k \geq 0}$ and $(m_k)_{k \geq 0}$ fulfilling that $x_k \in \bigcap_{l=0}^{k+1} T^l(E)$ for every $k \geq 0$. In particular, the vector
	\[
	x^* := \lim_{k \to \infty} x_k = x-\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}T^n m_n,
	\]
	which is well-defined since $T^nm_n \in M_n$ for each $n \geq 1$ and the series $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}T^n m_n$ is thus convergent, fulfills that $x^* \in \bigcap_{l \geq 0}T^{l}(E)$. Moreover, notice that
	\[
	T^Lx^* = T^Lx - \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} T^{L+n}m_n \in M = \bigcap_{l \geq 0} T^{-l}(E),
	\]
	and hence $x^* \in \bigcap_{l \geq L}T^{-l}(E)$. Since $x \notin M$ and $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}T^{n}m_n \in M$, we finally have that $0_{\omega} \neq x^* \in \bigcap_{|n| \geq L}T^{-n}(E)$, concluding the proof.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Given an invertible operator $T$ on $\omega$ and a closed subspace of finite codimension $E \subset \omega$, it is possible that for every $L \geq 0$ the space $\bigcap_{|n| \geq L}T^{-n}(E)$ is finite-dimensional. For instance, if we denote by $(e_n)_{n \geq 1}$ the canonical basis of $\omega$ and by $(e_n^*)_{n \geq 1}$ the corresponding coordinate functionals, then we can consider the operator $T$ given by $Te_{2n} := e_{2(n-1)}$ for each $n \geq 2$, $Te_2 := e_1$, and $Te_{2n+1} := e_{2n+3}$ for each $n \geq 0$. Thus, for $E := \ker(e_1^*) = \ker(p_1)$, given any $l \geq 1$ we have that
	\[
	T^l(E)=\ker(e^*_{2l+1}) \quad \text{ and } \quad T^{-l}(E)=\ker(e^*_{2l})
	\]
	so that $\bigcap_{|n| \geq L} T^{-n}(E)$ is finite-dimensional for every $L \geq 1$. This example also shows that we can have the equality $\bigcap_{n\in \mathbb{Z}}T^{-n} (E) = \{0_{\omega}\}$. Note that, if we reorder the indices of the basis $(e_n)_{n \geq 1}$ using the set $\mathbb{Z}$ appropriately, then the operator $T$ coincides with the classical bilateral shift on $\mathbb{K}^{\mathbb{Z}}$.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: There is no (metrically) expansive operator on $\omega$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $T$ be an invertible operator on $\omega$. Given $k \in \mathbb{N}$, let
	\[
	E_k := \ker(p_k) = \{ x = ([x]_j)_{j \geq 1} \in \omega : [x]_j = 0 \text{ for } 1 \leq j \leq k \}.
	\]
	It follows from Theorem~\ref{The:intersect-|n|>=L} applied to the finite-codimensional subspace $E_k$ that there exist some integer $L \geq 0$ and some vector $x \in \omega \setminus \{0_{\omega}\}$ such that $p_k(T^nx) = 0$ for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $|n| \geq L$. By considering an enough small multiple of $x$ we can assume that $p_k(T^nx) < \frac{1}{2^{k}}$ for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $|n|<L$. Since $(p_l)_{l \geq 1}$ given by \eqref{eq:omega.seminorms} is an increasing sequence of seminorms, we have for the metric $d$ given by \eqref{eq:metric} and for every integer $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ that
	\[
	d(T^nx,0_{\omega}) = \sum_{l=1}^{\infty} \frac{\min\{ 1 , p_l(T^nx) \}}{2^{l}} \leq \frac{1}{2^{k}} \sum_{l=1}^{k} \frac{1}{2^l} + \sum_{l=k+1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{2^l} < \frac{1}{2^{k-1}}.
	\]
	Thus, for each $k \in \mathbb{N}$ there exists some $x \in \omega \setminus \{0_{\omega}\}$ such that $d(T^nx,0_{\omega}) < 2^{-k+1}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Arguing exactly as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{The:no.pos-exp.omega} we can deduce that $T$ is not an expansive operator with respect to $d$, and that $\omega$ does not admit expansive operators in the metric sense.
head: environment

label: The:X+omega.pos-exp
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $Y$ be a subspace of $X$ such that $X = Y \oplus M$. We consider the projections $P_Y : X\oplus\omega \longrightarrow Y$, $P_M : X\oplus\omega \longrightarrow M$ and  $P_{\omega} : X\oplus\omega \longrightarrow \omega$ such that for any vector $z \in X\oplus\omega$ we can write $z = P_Yz + P_Mz + P_{\omega}z$. We now define an operator $T$ on $X\oplus\omega$ by letting
	\[
	Tz := 2P_Yz + 2F_u(P_Mz) + [P_{\omega}z]_1 u_1 + B_e(P_{\omega}z) \quad \text{ for each } z \in X\oplus\omega,
	\] 
	where $F_u : M \longrightarrow M$ is the forward shift along $(u_k)_{k \geq 1}$ and $B_e : \omega \longrightarrow \omega$ is the backward shift on $\omega$ along its canonical basis $(e_k)_{k \geq 1}$. Then, the linear map $T$ is continuous since the projections $P_Y$, $P_M$ and $P_{\omega}$ are continuous, since the forward shift $F_u$ is continuous on $M$ by assumption, and since the backward shift $B_e$ is continuous on $\omega$. It remains to show that $T$ is positively expansive. To check this fact notice that, since $P_Y$ and $P_M$ are continuous, there exist a continuous seminorm $q$ on $X\oplus\omega$ and a constant $C>0$ such that
	\[
	\|P_Y z\|_X \leq C q(z) \quad \text{ and } \quad \|P_M z\|_X \leq C q(z) \quad \text{ for every } z \in X\oplus\omega.
	\]
	Thus, given any non-zero vector $z \in X\oplus\omega$ we have several  non-mutually exclusive possibilities:
	\begin{enumerate}[label=$\bullet$]
		\item If $P_Yz \neq 0_Y$, then we get that
		\[
		\|P_Y(T^nz)\|_X = 2^n \|P_Yz\|_X \quad \text{ for every } n \geq 1,
		\]
		which implies that $q(T^nz) \geq \frac{1}{C}\|P_Y(T^nz)\|_X \geq 2^n \frac{\|P_Yz\|_X}{C}$. We can then conclude that $q(T^nz) \to \infty$ when $n \to \infty$
		
		\item If $P_Mz \neq 0_M$, then we get $P_Mz = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} z_k u_k$ with some $z_{k_0} \neq 0$. Since $(u_k)_{k \geq 1}$ is a basic sequence, each coordinate functional $u_k^* : M \longrightarrow \mathbb{K}$ satisfies that
		\[
		\|u_k^*\| \leq \frac{2K}{\|u_k\|_X},
		\]
		where $K$ is the basis constant of $(u_k)_k$; see for instance \cite[Vol.~I, Section~1.b.]{LindestraussTza1977_book_classical}. We can then deduce that 
		\begin{align*}
			2^n |z_{k_0}| = \left|u_{k_0+n}^*(P_M(T^n z))\right| &\leq \|u_{k_0+n}^*\| \cdot \|P_M(T^n z)\|_X \\[5pt]
			& \leq \frac{2KC}{\inf_{k \geq 1} \|u_k\|_X} \cdot q(T^n z),
		\end{align*}
		which implies that $q(T^nz) \to \infty$ when $n \to \infty$.
		
		\item If $P_{\omega}z \neq 0_{\omega}$, then we get $P_{\omega}z = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} w_ke_k$ with some $w_{k_0} \neq 0$. In this case it suffices to remark that $T^{k_0}z$ will satisfy $P_M(T^{k_0}z) \neq 0_M$, and by the previous case we deduce that $q(T^nz) \to \infty$ when $n \to \infty$.
	\end{enumerate}
	In conclusion, we get that $q(T^nz) \to \infty$ for every $z \in X\oplus\omega \setminus \{0_{X \oplus \omega}\}$ so that for any translation-invariant metric $d$ inducing the topology of $X\oplus\omega$ there must exists some $c>0$ such that $d(T^nz,0_{X \oplus \omega}) \geq c$ for all sufficiently big $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

label: The:X+omega.exp
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
With the continuity of the backward shift assumption we have that the operator $T$ defined in Theorem~\ref{The:X+omega.pos-exp} is invertible. In fact, its inverse $T^{-1}$ is given by
	\[
	T^{-1}z = \frac{1}{2}P_Yz + \frac{1}{2}B_u(P_Mz) + [P_Mz]_1 e_1 + F_e(P_{\omega}z) \quad \text{ for each } z \in X\oplus\omega,
	\] 
	where $B_u : M \longrightarrow M$ is the backward shift along $(u_k)_{k \geq 1}$ and $F_e : \omega \longrightarrow \omega$ is the forward shift on $\omega$ along its canonical basis $(e_k)_{k \geq 1}$.
head: environment

title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: It suffices to remark that these spaces admit a basic sequence satisfying the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{The:X+omega.exp}. If $X=\ell^p$ for $p \in [1,\infty[$ or $c_0$, we can let $(u_k)_{k \geq 1}$ be its canonical basis. If $X$ is an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, it suffices to consider any orthonormal sequence $(u_k)_{k \geq 1}$ in $X$. Finally, if $X$ is a non-reflexive Banach space admitting an unconditional basis, using James~\cite{James1950_AnnalsMath_bases} we know that $X$ contains a complemented copy of $\ell^1$ or a complemented copy of $c_0$.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md: The spaces $\omega(\ell^p)$ with $p\in [1,\infty[$ and $\omega(c_0)$ admit an invertible positively expansive operator and thus an expansive operator.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $X=\ell^p$ with $p\in [1,\infty[$ or $c_0$ and denote by $(e_n)_{n \geq 1}$ the canonical basis of such space. Let $(A_j)_{j \geq 1}$ be a partition of $\mathbb{N}$ where each set $A_j$ is infinite. For each $j \geq 1$, we denote by $(n_{j,k})_{k \geq 1}$ the increasing enumeration of $A_j$ and we then consider the operator $F_A$ defined on $X$ by 
	\[
	F_A\left(\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}x_{n_{j,k}} e_{n_{j,k}}\right)=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}x_{n_{j,k}} e_{n_{j+1,k}}.
	\]
	In other words, we identify $X$ with an infinity copy of itself and $F_A$ is the forward shift along these copies. In the same way, we define the operator $B_A$ on $X$ by
	\[
	B_A\left(\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}x_{n_{j,k}} e_{n_{j,k}}\right)=\sum_{j=2}^{\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}x_{n_{j,k}} e_{n_{j-1,k}}.
	\]
	We now consider the operator $T : \omega(X) \longrightarrow \omega(X)$ given by
	\[
	Tx := \left(2F_A(x^{(1)})+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} [x^{(2)}]_k e_{n_{1,k}}, x^{(3)}, x^{(4)}, x^{(5)}, \dots \right),
	\]
	for each $x = (x^{(j)})_{j \geq 1} \in \omega(X)$. This operator is continuous on $\omega(X)$ and is even invertible. In fact, it is not hard to check that
	\[
	T^{-1}x = \left( \frac{1}{2}B_A(x^{(1)}), \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} [x^{(1)}]_{n_{1,k}} e_k, x^{(2)}, x^{(3)}, x^{(4)}, \dots \right),
	\]
	for each $x = (x^{(j)})_{j \geq 1} \in \omega(X)$. Moreover the operator $T$ is positively expansive since for every vector $x = (x^{(j)})_{j \geq 1} \in \omega(X) \setminus \{0_{\omega(X)}\}$ we get that $p_1(T^n x)$ tends to infinity. Indeed, if $x = (x^{(j)})_{j \geq 1}$ is a non-zero vector in $\omega(X)$, there exists $j_0 \geq 1$ such that $x^{(j_0)}$ is different to $0_X$ and we then have $p_1(T^{j_0-1}x) \neq 0$. Moreover, for every $n \geq 0$ and every $x \in \omega(X)$ we have, by the definition of $T$, that
	\[
	p_1(T^n x) \geq 2^np_1(x).
	\]
	We then get the desired conclusion.
